name: Manatee
lede: Manatee is a cool, purplish grey named for the skin of the aquatic mammal, a muted color meant to evoke a creature often called a sea cow.

sections.title: A sea mammal's grey
sections.body:
Our library traces the name only to a Wikipedia color list, with no date for its coining [1]. In printed English the word "manatee" (as an adjective, the color sense) peaked in the 1980s and rose fastest from the 1950s, well after the animal's own long-known name [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[dutch-blue]], 4.1 units of CIEDE2000 away and bluer [1]. [[plumbago-grey]] sits almost as close, at 4.4, described as almost the same, and [[deep-plumbago-blue]] at 4.8, lighter [1]. Measured in LCH, Manatee sits at lightness 64 with very low chroma, a true neutral with only a faint purple cast [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 283 of 23,781 paintings (1.2 percent), more common than 65 percent of the named colors, as photographed [2]. Claude Monet is its most devoted painter, using it in 7 of the 50 Monet works here, 9.7 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [2]. It peaks in the 1930s, in 5 of 69 paintings, at 4.5 times the expected rate, and most often plays a light inside a painting, 49 percent of the time [2]. Werner's 1821 nomenclature lists a related entry, Bluish Purple, exemplified by parts of the white and purple crocus, within 6.4 units of this swatch [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [2].
